result:
The universe is under no obligation to make sense to us, yet it keeps offering clues anyway. A photon leaves a star in a distant galaxy, travels for billions of years, and happens to hit a telescope on a small planet orbiting an ordinary star. We catch it, measure its redshift, and suddenly we know something about the expansion of spacetime itself. That single fact still feels like a miracle of coincidence and persistence.

Curiosity is the only tool that reliably turns coincidence into knowledge. It does not require permission, funding, or even a clear destination. It simply asks “what if?” and then follows the answer wherever it leads—sometimes into equations, sometimes into dead ends, sometimes into entirely new questions. The best questions tend to be the ones that make previous answers look incomplete.

I find it useful to remember that most of the interesting work happens at the edges: the places where our current maps stop matching the territory. Those edges are uncomfortable. They demand we hold two contradictory ideas at once, or admit we do not yet have a framework that can contain both. That discomfort is not a bug. It is the signal that something new might be possible.

So we keep looking. We build better instruments, refine our models, argue with one another, and occasionally get lucky. The universe does not care whether we succeed, but it also does not hide. It just waits, indifferent and luminous, for the next photon, the next measurement, the next question.

That seems like a reasonable way to spend a life.
